title: Evaling Video Slop — Maor Bril, Character.ai
talk_summary: Maor Bril describes building a fast, small VLM judge for AI-generated video at Character.ai, replacing a slow pipeline of frame metrics plus frontier-LLM judges with a distilled pairwise-comparison model that explains *why* a video is bad. Key transferable ideas: relative (A vs B) scoring instead of absolute 1-10, scoring the specific axes you care about, putting evals inside the generation loop, and calibrating judges with periodic human annotation.

takeaways.technique: Pairwise relative judging instead of absolute scores
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of asking a judge to score 1-10 (where humans and models disagree wildly), they train/ask for A-vs-B comparisons, which are far more consistent and generalizable.
takeaways.evidence_quote: don't score compare... if I show you two videos and I'll ask you which one of them is telling a better story, the grand majority will probably agree

takeaways.technique: Score the real axes, not the vibe
takeaways.what_they_do: Their v1 judge learned to detect 'coherent video' and 'AI artifacts' (the vibe) rather than the actual axes (story, physics, pacing, audio sync), so it confidently scored a still image 9.2 on camera work. Fix was to restructure the dataset/annotation around explicit axes.

takeaways.technique: Put eval inside the generation loop, catch defects early
takeaways.what_they_do: They moved evaluation as close to generation as possible (even scoring starting frames before video generation) because catching a defect early is much cheaper than after the full artifact is assembled.

takeaways.technique: Distill a committee of experts into one small fast model
takeaways.what_they_do: They replaced a slow, expensive pipeline (frame metrics + frontier LLM judges + human calibration) with a small fine-tuned VLM that scores a 15s video in ~3s and outputs reasons, not just a verdict. They explicitly chose the smaller model because the bigger model's quality gain didn't justify the latency.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it takes about 3 seconds to score a three 15 second video... the added value from the bigger model didn't justify the the the the slowness
takeaways.numbers: ~3s per 15s video for small VLM; bigger model better but significantly slower

takeaways.technique: Periodic human annotation to calibrate AI judges
takeaways.what_they_do: Every generated report can be human-annotated; they run short 10-15 min team annotation sessions on random axes and feed that back to calibrate the LLM judge and as training data for the next model version.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we will periodically have sessions where everyone spends 10 to 15 minutes just annotating videos... I use the data to to calibrate the the AI judges

takeaways.technique: Agentic workflow with validation tools beats rigid pipeline
takeaways.what_they_do: They moved from a fixed pipeline to an agentic workflow where agents get tools to validate their own outputs, because pipelines break once real users bring varied inputs; agents can verify and fix as they go.
takeaways.evidence_quote: by providing the agents with tools to validate the quality of of the outputs it's creating, it's able to adapt to changes better. It's also able to verify its own work
